RagShortTexts: Milanese commerce and craft depend on Lombard agriculture, routes and demand for equipment.
Full articulated plate armour is not standard workshop equipment in 1259.

Variants.Content: Milan stood amid the productive lands and routes of Lombardy, where grain, fodder and craft production supported a wealthy commune. Its metalworkers made mail, helmets and other arms, with construction varying by workshop and patron; a complete articulated plate harness should not be projected onto every Milanese soldier in 1259. Water-powered hammers and later manufacturing traditions must likewise be tied to evidence for particular places and dates, rather than treated as uniform guild practice. Milanese politics involved competing urban factions, including the Torriani and Visconti, but the Visconti did not establish durable supremacy until later in the thirteenth century.

A Milanese smith depends on sound iron, fuel, tools and repeated work at the hearth. In 1259 armour making centres on the equipment of the period, including mail, helmets and reinforcing pieces. The articulated full plate harness of a later age must not be placed on every workshop bench. Fit and repair matter even when a patron pays for elaborate decoration.

Going into battle in Milanese mail gives a soldier real confidence, because the links are close and the plates sit well on the body. Heavy crossbow quarrels glance off the cold-worked iron. Armour does not save a man who breaks ranks, though, so keep your shield up and your place in the line.
